title: Metatables and sortable items
summary: Teach two tables how to compare and print through metamethods, then repair a sort that has no ordering rule.

objectives.description: Find a sort that has no comparison metamethod.
Reason about equal elements under table.sort.

hints: Metamethods are looked up on the metatable.
Item.__index = Item shares methods with every instance.
__lt receives the left and right operands.

misconceptions.description: Sorting tables without a comparison metamethod.
misconceptions.feedback: table.sort compares elements with <. Two plain tables have no <, so sort raises an error. Define __lt on their shared metatable.

misconceptions.description: Expecting table.sort to keep equal elements stable.
misconceptions.feedback: table.sort is not stable. When __lt is false in both directions, either order is valid, so add a tie-breaker when order matters.

misconceptions.description: Defining a separate metatable per item.
misconceptions.testDescription: Items compare by count and then by name.
misconceptions.feedback: One shared metatable keeps behavior consistent and cheap. Per-item metatables make the ordering rule harder to reason about.

misconceptions.description: Storing a new closure on every item.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Attaching a fresh __lt closure to each item table instead of using the shared Item metatable.
misconceptions.feedback: Methods belong on the shared metatable. Store data on the item and behavior on Item.

sections.title: Metatables intercept operations
sections.body: A metatable is an ordinary table that changes how another table behaves. setmetatable(item, Item) attaches it. __index handles missing keys, __tostring controls tostring, __eq compares equality, and __lt defines the less-than relation. Lua looks these names up on the metatable when the operation occurs.

sections.title: Comparison needs a strict order
sections.body: table.sort(arr) uses the < operator between elements. For tables, that means __lt must exist and must define a consistent order. If two elements are not less than each other in either direction, they are equivalent for sorting; the algorithm may place them in either order. Add a name tie-breaker when the report must be deterministic.

sections.title: Share behavior, store data
sections.body: Set Item.__index = Item so instances fall back to the module table for methods. Define Item.new(name, count) to build the data and attach the metatable. Avoid giving every instance its own closures; shared methods are easier to test and use less memory.

vocabulary.definition: A function on a metatable that Lua calls for an operator or conversion.
The metamethod that implements the less-than comparison.
The metamethod that supplies the string used by tostring.
A sort that preserves the input order of elements that compare equal.

steps.title: Order and print inventory items
steps.prompt: Edit main.lua. Define __lt so items sort by count and then name, and __tostring so each row reads name:count.
hints: __lt receives left and right item tables.
Use string.format("%s:%d", item.name, item.count) for display.

localVerification.description: Runs the file with Lua, which calls the metamethods during sort and printing.

tests.description: Items compare by count and then by name.
The sort and display loop are intact.

steps.title: The sort with no order
steps.prompt: table.sort raises "attempt to compare two table values". Select the faulty instruction and the correct repair.
hints: The items are tables, so < must be defined.
Define __lt on the shared Item metatable.

fixes.label: Define Item.__lt(left, right) on the shared metatable.
Convert every item to a string before sorting.

steps.explanation: Plain tables have no built-in order. table.sort uses <, so the metatable needs __lt. Converting the items to strings changes the data instead of teaching it how to compare.

steps.title: Equal counts in a sort
steps.prompt: Two items have the same count, and __lt returns false in both directions. What does table.sort do with them?
hints: Neither element is less than the other.
The comparator sees them as equivalent.

quiz.prompt: Two items have the same count, and __lt returns false in both directions. What does table.sort do with them?

options.label: Treats them as equivalent and may place either one first.
Raises an error because the order is ambiguous.
Keeps the earlier item first because Lua sorts stably.
Removes one of the equal items.

quiz.explanation: table.sort only knows what __lt reports. Equal elements are interchangeable to the algorithm, and Lua does not promise a stable result, so a tie-breaker is needed for a deterministic report.
